transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-28
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~70 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE - joined late), Mark Rivera (Atlas Head of ML), Sasha Li (Atlas Platform), Tom Becker (Atlas Security), Ivy Chen (Atlas SRE)

Summary: Technical deep dive on benchmark methodology focused on runtime apples-to-apples comparisons, KV cache behaviour, batching strategies, quantization impact, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed next steps: share harness, submit traffic profile and prompt sets, run pilot in VPC env.

Transcript:
00:00 Alex: alright hi everyone thanks for joining, um this is Alex from Redwood inference, im the AE on the account, with me is Priya our SE who will drive the methodology part of today s workshop, and Jordan might pop on later.
00:07 Mark: hey thanks alex, Sasha Tom Ivy from Atlas here, we re mainly trying to understand how to run apples to apples benchmarks between our current hosted provider and Redwood, and also how things behave inside our VPC/on-prem.
00:15 Priya: perfect, yeah we ll cover prompt sets, load generation, metrics to capture, and some common pitfalls re caching and quantization. this is fairly similar to other pilots we ve run with healthcare customers.
00:24 Sasha: quick note — we have strict P95 latency goals for interactive features (~250ms) and batched async workloads for summarization we care about throughput and cost. also security: we need audit logs and KMS integration.
00:35 Tom: and for legal we need data residency plus SOC2/ISO stuff, but that s more paperwork, want to get the numbers first.
00:42 Priya: totally. first slide — benchmark philosophy: apples-to-apples means same model version, same tokenization, same sequence length distribution, equivalent batching policy and KV cache warm state. a few quick gotchas: 1) many public benchmarks forget prefix caching (KV) which favors cold-run performance; 2) quantization can change per-token timing and memory footprint; 3) network and region hops matter for VPC runs.
01:05 Mark: can you give a concrete example for the KV thing? sometimes I see vendors claim crazy tps but when we try it our latency jumps after 10k tokens.
01:12 Priya: yeah so KV cache is stateful — if you re doing many short-turn interactions and the runtime is doing prefix caching, your effective per-token latency is lower after the cache is warm. if the benchmark is synthetic and always cold-starts each request you re not measuring warm path. also some runtimes evict KV more aggressively under memory pressure, which changes tail latency.
01:30 Sasha: so for a fair comparison we should replicate our real session distribution, not just a single long convo or single prompt repeated, right?
01:36 Priya: exactly. we recommend capturing 3 canonical prompt sets: interactive chat (avg tokens per request 40, session length distribution X), long generation (single prompt -> 800 tokens), and batch embeddings/summary workloads. also provide session-level traces so we can replay prefix warmup.
01:55 Alex: on the runner side we ll share our benchmark harness — it can replay sessions, enforce concurrency, and simulate KV warm/cold states. note that load generator configuration matters: virtual users vs open-loop RPS, backpressure handling etc.
02:10 Mark: what about batching — how do you pick the batch size? our current provider uses dynamic batching and claims low latency, but costs spike.
02:18 Priya: batching tradeoffs are workload and SLO dependent. for low-latency interactive you generally prefer smaller batches with stricter latency SLOs; for throughput-y jobs you can increase batch sizes to amortize kernel overhead. our harness supports per-model batch policies so we can emulate your current provider's batching and compare cost/latency curves.
02:36 Priya: also important is the kernel selection and quantization path — e.g., int8 quant vs fp16 changes memory and sometimes changes per-token compute. some GPUs have specialized tensor cores that favor certain quant paths; we ll note that in the result set.
02:48 Sasha: we run on NVIDIA A10G on prem for now; planning to try dedicated cloud gpus later. any known gotchas for A10G and int8?
02:56 Priya: A10G supports efficient fp16 and some int8 paths but quantized performance varies by model architecture. we ll add a quantization matrix to the report: model vs quantization vs expected throughput and recommended kernel.
03:08 Tom: security question: if we run the pilot in our VPC how do you instrument network egress? we need to ensure no data leaves the VPC and KMS keys stay with us.
03:18 Alex: for Redwood Private in VPC mode the inference nodes run in your account or on-prem — keys stay in your KMS and audit logs are forwarded to your SIEM. we ll share our security checklist; Priya will help map bench hooks so logs include request ids and token-level timing for traceability.
03:33 Ivy: and what about telemetry overhead — will the instrumentation affect latency numbers?
03:39 Priya: minimal if you sample appropriately. we recommend capturing full traces for a subset of runs and aggregated metrics for load tests; we ll document the measurement overhead in the harness README.
03:49 Mark: ok can you walk through an end-to-end scenario — we want to compare our current hosted service vs Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private in our VPC, measure cost per 1M tokens, and P95 latency across 3 prompt sets.
04:01 Priya: yeah end-to-end plan: 1) Atlas provides canonical prompt sets + traffic distribution; 2) we run baseline on your hosted provider using the harness (you ll run or let us run if you provide credentials); 3) we run Redwood Hosted with same config; 4) we run Redwood Dedicated (our reserved capacity) and Redwood Private in your VPC/on-prem; 5) compare metrics: median, P50, P95 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, and cost per token breakdown. we ll also provide KV warm vs cold split.
04:36 Sasha: for cost calculations do you include amortized infra costs and idle tail? some vendors discount peak utilization but hide idle costs.
04:44 Alex: yes we include amortized reserved capacity, GPU hours, and inference runtime overhead. for Dedicated we show both committed and burst scenarios so you can see the utilization sensitivity.
04:55 Mark: what about randomness in model outputs affecting token length? if one model generates longer continuations it changes tokens per request and costs — how do you normalize?
05:04 Priya: good point: we normalize to tokens produced and also report per-call metrics. we can fix max generation tokens across runs to get apples-to-apples, and also run open-ended generation to measure realistic cost distribution. both will be in the methodology.
05:18 Jordan (joins): hey all — sorry late. just to add, we usually also collect kernel-level counters and GPU mem/SM utilization to diagnose bottlenecks, and we log model weights size and quant artifacts.
05:29 Tom: do you have examples of previous healthcare pilots? any notes on compliance constraints?
05:34 Priya: yes we ran a pilot with MedCore last year — key takeaways: warm KV eliminated ~40% of token cost on chat flows, quantization saved 30-50% in GPU memory enabling doubling batch size for throughput jobs, and VPC mode required an extra 2-3 days for KMS integration and security scanning. we ll anonymize that report and share relevant sections.
05:56 Sasha: awesome. about the harness — will it be runnable in our air-gapped environment?
06:02 Priya: the harness is a python runner with a small dependency set; we can provide a tarball and offline docs. for air-gapped/on-prem we ship a packaged runner and a small agent to push metrics to your graphite/prometheus or to local files for collection.
06:18 Mark: any pitfalls we should look out for when redoing our current provider tests to be fair?
06:22 Priya: common mistakes: 1) letting the provider auto-scale to huge instance types when comparing to a reserved GPU; 2) not reproducing the same tokenization and model version; 3) ignoring KV cache warm states; 4) measuring only median not P95 and P99.
06:38 Alex: ok looks like alignment — next we ll exchange the bench harness link and you ll share prompt sets. we ll schedule the VPC pilot with Atlas infra.
06:46 Mark: sounds good; also please include a short doc on recommended autoscaling policies for Dedicated to hit our P95 target while controlling cost.
06:52 Alex: will do. quick recap: Priya shares harness + README + example load generator; Mark shares traffic profile and prompt sets; Tom confirms security checklist items for VPC; Alex sends Dedicated pricing and config. Plan to reconvene after initial baseline runs — propose 2026-02-11 for a results review.
06:59 Tom: ok thanks everyone.
07:00 End of call

References shared during call:
